description: The team for g10 in Ajman american private school
summary:
Fire behaves strangely in space. With no buoyancy there's no flame to watch dance upward, just a dim, round glow that lingers and hides. Most people have never seen it, so we built a place where you can. Drag the gravity slider from freefall to Earth and the flame changes shape in front of you; turn up the oxygen and it gets hotter, dirtier and faster.

Everything behind that is real. We went through NASA's combustion research and pulled out 24 experiments, from decades of ISS work to a candle that burned for 45 minutes on Mir, each one with its facility, its years and a link to the actual source. Nothing is made up. On top of that, a what-if simulator lets you try cabin setups and suppression tactics, and an AI co-pilot answers your questions by quoting those experiments back at you, with the IDs, so you can check its work.

One thing stuck with us: NASA's own results show the standard fire test for spacecraft materials is too optimistic, and some flames keep burning long after the visible fire goes out. That felt worth making impossible to ignore.
details:
Flame in Freefall pulls together a bunch of NASA studies on how fire behaves without gravity into one interactive setup. It lets users dig through experiments and materials while looking at mission scenarios that might come up later on longer trips. The timeline part shows how some of those discoveries built on each other over time.

There is a chamber that compares flames on Earth to what happens in microgravity and that helps make the differences clearer. An AI assistant pulls answers from the research collection when people ask questions about it. I think the whole thing tries to make the science less distant and maybe spark more interest in space work but fire safety challenges still feel pretty big for moon or mars missions.

The mix of 3D visuals with the research database and AI is what stands out instead of keeping everything in separate reports. They used React and Three js along with some other tools to build it and tried to keep things accurate and easy to use during development. It seems like an independent prototype so it is not meant to replace any official systems.
dataRefs: NASA Physical Science Informatics (primary data source)
